signal: Today’s strongest signal is that agent quality and cost are increasingly being set by the training and runtime contracts around the model: harnesses can auto-optimize themselves, observation tokens shape RL exploration, stop-token semantics can destabilize distillation, agent latency depends on task-aware local scheduling, and hidden behavioral transfer remains hard to scrub from training data.

stories.title: SoL-Pi auto-discovers agent-harness changes that cut token traffic nearly in half
stories.summary: SoL-Pi applies recursive auto-research to the coding-agent harness itself, searching across increasingly diverse environments for reusable runtime improvements. Four mechanisms survive selection—action execution, context compaction, observation handling and delegated reading. On the 51-task EdgeBench evaluation, the authors report performance comparable to Pi across GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 while reducing recorded token traffic by 44.7–49.0% and API cost by about one third.
stories.whyItMatters: This makes the harness an optimization target rather than fixed plumbing. If model quality is held roughly constant, large gains can come from changing how context is compacted, observations are presented, tools are invoked and reading is delegated. For teams running coding or research agents at scale, the practical pattern is similar to profile-guided optimization: automatically search runtime policies, but promote only changes that survive held-out tasks and regression checks.
stories.attention: Very high — agent runtimes can now be optimized recursively for cost and context efficiency without changing the underlying model

stories.title: ActObs trains agents on environment observations and improves downstream RL exploration
stories.summary: ActObs changes a small but consequential convention in agent supervised fine-tuning: instead of applying loss only to agent-authored actions, it also supervises the environment-observation tokens already present in each trajectory. It adds no new data, parameters, sequence tokens or forward passes. After GRPO, Qwen3-4B improves pass@k at every evaluated sampling budget on Terminal-Bench 2.0; Qwen3-8B gains 3.4 percentage points at pass@16, and the 4B model improves aider-polyglot pass@1 by 4.2 points.
stories.whyItMatters: Trajectory preprocessing is part of the learning algorithm. Masking observations teaches the model what to do but not what its actions cause; supervising them preserves consequence prediction and appears to leave more useful entropy for later RL exploration. Teams building tool-using agents should treat action and observation loss masks as a first-class training choice rather than a harmless implementation default.
stories.attention: Very high — a zero-extra-data change to SFT supervision materially changes how well agents explore under later reinforcement learning

stories.title: EOS-token mismatch can make on-policy-distilled models run excessively long
stories.summary: A new study traces one source of length inflation in on-policy distillation to termination-token mismatch between the base student and post-trained teacher. Across Qwen3, Llama and Gemma, teacher and student can place stopping probability on different EOS tokens even when their declared stopping sets are identical. Aligning the decoding stop set alone is insufficient; treating functionally equivalent EOS tokens as one semantic stopping action substantially reduces mismatch-induced inflation across all three families.
stories.whyItMatters: Stop behavior is a protocol contract, not merely a tokenizer detail. A distillation pipeline can appear to preserve task quality while silently producing longer outputs, higher latency and larger inference bills because teacher and student disagree about which token means 'done.' Model-training stacks should normalize semantic termination across tokenizers and monitor response-length distributions throughout post-training, not only final accuracy or reward.
stories.attention: High — token-level termination semantics can create system-level cost and latency regressions during distillation

stories.title: Agent serving needs task-aware resource scheduling, not simply faster models
stories.summary: Researchers profiled RAG, web-search and coding agents that mix remote LLM calls with local tool containers and found sharply different CPU, disk-I/O and memory behavior across tasks—even when the same tool is used. Faster model responses or more CPU cores do not always reduce end-to-end latency. CPU-aware tool admission and task-aware CPU allocation improved CPU-sensitive task latency by about 5.4× and reduced average latency across mixed tasks by about 32% versus native agents.
stories.whyItMatters: Agent latency is a distributed-systems problem spanning model endpoints and local execution. Scaling the LLM tier while leaving tool containers unmanaged can simply move the bottleneck. Production agent platforms need per-tool resource profiles, admission control, backpressure and task-aware CPU allocation so orchestration decisions reflect the whole trajectory rather than only model-token throughput.
stories.attention: High — the resource scheduler around tools can dominate agent latency even when model inference gets faster

stories.title: Training-data attribution does not reliably filter subliminal learning
stories.summary: A safety study tests whether gradient-based data-attribution methods can remove 'subliminal learning,' where models transmit behavioral traits through training examples with no obvious semantic relationship to those traits. Token-level EK-FAC mitigates a significant part of the effect, but GradCos variants provide little benefit and all methods mostly trail a stronger divergence-token baseline. Filtering entire samples is weaker still, and success varies substantially across model–preference combinations.
stories.whyItMatters: Semantic content filters are not enough when behavioral information can hide in data that looks innocuous, and generic attribution is not yet a dependable replacement. Synthetic-data and distillation pipelines need provenance, behavioral holdout tests and model-specific auditing rather than assuming that suspicious examples can be identified after the fact with one attribution score.
stories.attention: High — hidden behavioral transfer remains difficult to detect and sanitize reliably in model-generated training data

takeaway: Treat trajectories, termination semantics, resource profiles and training-data provenance as first-class interfaces. Optimize the harness and scheduler as aggressively as the model, supervise agents on the consequences already present in their traces, normalize stop actions across teacher–student stacks, and do not assume attribution alone can sanitize synthetic or distilled data.
